_meta.description: Manual GM-style action-oriented labels for all SAE features. Each label describes the IDEA/PLAN the player should execute, not the board state.
_meta.method: Analyzed top-5 activating positions per feature, identified the common strategic/tactical idea that determines the correct continuation.

257.label: Calculate concrete variations — the position demands precise calculation
257.description: Positions across all phases where the right move requires concrete calculation (not intuition). Captures available, checks possible, tactical motifs present. The player must calculate forcing sequences accurately.

431.label: Strike in the center — seize the initiative with a central break or piece maneuver
431.description: White to move with d4+e4 center and developed pieces. The key idea is to break open the center NOW while ahead in development (Bc4+Nc3+Nf3 ready). Delay means Black equalizes.

74.label: Punish the opponent's lag in development — convert tempo advantage into attack
74.description: White to move with superior development. The idea is to open the position before the opponent catches up. Look for pawn breaks, piece sacrifices, or forcing lines that exploit the uncastled king or undeveloped pieces.

430.label: Defend accurately under pressure — find the only move that holds
430.description: Black to move in positions where White has the initiative. Multiple captures and tactical threats exist. The key is finding precise defensive moves (counter-threats, simplifications, or resource moves) rather than panicking.

156.label: Use the centralized knight — the outpost knight dominates, play around it
156.description: Black has a powerful knight on d5 (or similar outpost). The idea: don't trade it. Instead, use it as an anchor to restrict White's pieces and launch operations on the wing where you have more space. The knight is your most valuable piece.

295.label: Simplify and convert — trade pieces to reach a winning endgame
295.description: Positions where one side has an advantage (material, structure, or activity). The key idea is to SIMPLIFY — trade pieces, reduce complexity, and convert the edge into a technical win. Avoid complications that let the opponent back in.

103.label: Keep the position solid — don't rush, improve piece placement gradually
103.description: Black to move in solid but slightly passive positions. The idea is prophylaxis and gradual improvement — don't create weaknesses trying to equalize immediately. Move pieces to better squares, maintain pawn structure integrity.

380.label: Dominate through superior piece coordination — win the tactical skirmish
380.description: Dense middlegame with multiple minor pieces in combat. Many captures available. The idea: coordinate your pieces to work together (discovered attacks, double attacks, piece chains) while disrupting opponent coordination.

150.label: Target the opponent's weak squares — plant pieces on holes in their pawn structure
150.description: Positions where one side has structural weaknesses (backward pawns, holes). The idea is to occupy those weak squares with pieces (especially knights) and build pressure on the weak pawns. Positional domination.

243.label: Initiate concrete threats — look for tactics before the opponent consolidates
243.description: Positions with high tactical tension. Many captures and checks available for Black. The key: don't just develop — create specific threats (forks, pins, discovered attacks) that force the opponent to react to YOU.

83.label: Bring the king into the game — king activity decides the endgame
83.description: Simplified positions where the king must become an active piece. Walk the king toward the center or toward passed pawns. In endgames, the king is worth roughly 4 pawns in fighting value. Don't leave it passive.

449.label: Find the killer blow — the position is ripe for a decisive attack
449.description: Positions where a direct attack on the king is the primary idea. Sacrifices may be required. Look for queen + piece coordination targeting weak squares around the enemy king. Calculate the mating net.

215.label: Exploit the fianchetto bishop — use the long diagonal as your primary weapon
215.description: White has Bg2 or Bb2 on the long diagonal. The idea: open the diagonal (trade or advance center pawns), build battery with queen behind bishop, and target the opponent's queenside/kingside along the diagonal.

510.label: Penetrate with queen and rooks — break into the opponent's back ranks
510.description: The key idea is heavy piece invasion. Get your queen/rooks to the 2nd/1st rank (or 7th/8th for Black). This creates back-rank mating threats and attacks undefended pawns. Look for open files and weak back rank.

440.label: Find the unexpected defensive or counterattacking resource
440.description: Positions where the best move is non-obvious — a quiet defensive move, an unexpected sacrifice, or a counter-intuitive retreat. The idea: look beyond natural moves for the move that changes the evaluation.

96.label: Apply precise technique — no room for creativity, just accuracy
96.description: Very simplified positions (K+R, K+Q, K+P). The idea is pure technique: opposition, triangulation, cutting off the king, promoting passed pawns. Every move must be precise — one slip and the advantage evaporates.

452.label: Blunt the opponent's attack — counter-punch rather than passively defend
452.description: White to move facing Black's active piece play. The idea: don't just defend — find counter-threats that force the opponent to worry about THEIR position. The best defense is often a counter-attack in the center.

497.label: Rook endgame technique — get the rook behind the passed pawn
497.description: Rook endgame positions. The fundamental idea: place your rook BEHIND passed pawns (yours or the opponent's). Cut off the enemy king with your rook. Advance passed pawns with the rook supporting from behind.

68.label: Finish development and castle — don't grab pawns at the cost of development
68.description: Opening positions where the key idea is completing development harmoniously. Don't get distracted by pawn grabs or premature attacks. Develop pieces to natural squares, castle, connect rooks. Solid development first.

174.label: Place pieces on dominant central squares — control the board from the center
174.description: The idea is piece centralization. Move knights to d4/e5, bishops to active diagonals, rooks to central files. A centralized piece is worth more than a passive one. The center controls everything.

75.label: Storm the kingside with pawns — advance h/g pawns to open lines against the king
75.description: Positions where the center is closed/stable. The idea: advance pawns on the wing where you're attacking (h4-h5, g4-g5). Open files and diagonals pointing at the enemy king. The pawn storm creates the breach.

119.label: Refute the opponent's overextension — counter-strike when they overreach
119.description: White to move facing Black's aggressive but premature piece play. The key: the opponent has weakened their position by attacking too early. Find the move that exploits their overextension (central break, piece fork, counter-sacrifice).

381.label: Select the correct pawn break to open the position favorably
381.description: Positions where the pawn structure is locked or semi-locked. The idea: identify which pawn break (d4, e4, c4, f4, etc.) will open the position to YOUR advantage. The right break at the right time is the key to these positions.

291.label: Double rooks or create queen+rook battery on an open file
291.description: The idea is heavy piece coordination. Double your rooks on an open file, put the queen behind them, or create a battery targeting a weakness. Heavy pieces are strongest when they work together on the same file or rank.

116.label: Restrict the opponent's pieces — slowly improve your position while they're cramped
116.description: Positions with space advantage (e4+g3 setup or similar). The idea: don't rush. Improve your worst piece, restrict the opponent's movement, prepare a pawn break only when fully ready. The squeeze strategy.

34.label: Push your center pawns forward — the mobile center is your main weapon
34.description: Black has strong center pawns (d5+e5 or similar). The idea: advance them at the right moment to gain space, open lines for your pieces, and restrict the opponent. The pawn center is a battering ram.

198.label: March the king to the center — in endgames, the king must fight
198.description: Simplified positions where king activity is THE deciding factor. The idea: bring your king to the center or toward the critical sector immediately. Every tempo matters — the first king to arrive wins.

226.label: Count tempi in the pawn race — one move decides everything
226.description: Pure or near-pure pawn endings. The idea: count exactly. Who promotes first? Can you create a passed pawn? Is there opposition? Zugzwang? Every single move must be calculated — intuition fails here.

329.label: Strike while the king is in the center — open lines before they castle
329.description: The opponent's king hasn't castled. The idea: open the center immediately with pawn breaks or piece sacrifices. Every move they spend NOT castling is a move you can use to increase your attack. Urgency is key.

168.label: Seek active counterplay — use piece activity to create threats rather than defending passively
168.description: Black to move in sharp middlegames with multiple captures and checks available. The idea: look for active moves (checks, captures, counter-threats) rather than passive defense. The best defense is a counter-attack.

235.label: Complete development and consolidate — connect rooks and prepare the middlegame plan
235.description: Black to move in standard middlegame positions with full development. The idea: identify the right plan based on pawn structure. Dont move pieces aimlessly — each move should serve a concrete strategic purpose.

353.label: Prepare and execute the right pawn break in the center
353.description: White to move in positions where the pawn structure is semi-closed. The idea: prepare a central pawn break (e4, d4, c4, f4) to open lines for your pieces. Timing is critical — break too early and you weaken yourself.

391.label: Understand the pawn structure — it dictates piece placement and plans
391.description: Mixed positions where pawn structure is the key feature. The idea: read the pawn skeleton to determine where your pieces belong, which side to play on, and what the long-term plan should be.

181.label: Create and advance a passed pawn — the most powerful endgame weapon
181.description: Simplified positions where creating a passed pawn is the key idea. Look for pawn majorities, pawn breaks that create passers, and then advance them with king support. A passed pawn is worth a piece in some endgames.

73.label: Use space advantage to restrict and squeeze the opponent
73.description: White to move with advanced pawns (often e5 or d5) creating space. The idea: dont rush to attack. Instead, improve your worst piece while the opponent is cramped. They will eventually create a weakness you can target.

281.label: Evaluate whether to accept or decline a sacrifice — calculate precisely
281.description: Black to move facing White piece aggression with multiple captures and checks available. The idea: when offered material, calculate whether accepting is safe. Sometimes declining and simplifying is stronger than a greedy capture.

7.label: Use rook activity to defend — a passive rook loses, an active rook draws or wins
7.description: Black to move with rook(s) in simplified positions. The key principle: keep your rook ACTIVE even when defending. An active rook on the 2nd/7th rank creates perpetual threats that prevent the opponent from converting.

123.label: Dont rush to resolve tension — maintain it while improving your position
123.description: White to move in positions with significant piece tension. The idea: resist the urge to capture or exchange immediately. Sometimes the THREAT of capture is stronger than the capture itself. Improve first, then strike.

464.label: Calculate the pawn race precisely — count tempi to determine who promotes first
464.description: Simplified positions with pawns racing to promote. The idea: count moves precisely. Who gets a queen first? Can you promote with check? Can you sacrifice to deflect? The pawn race calculation must be exact.

193.label: Deliver the finishing blow — calculate the winning combination
193.description: White to move with overwhelming piece activity. Many captures and checks available. The idea: this is a forced win — find the exact sequence. Dont settle for a small advantage when a knockout blow exists.

209.label: Develop pieces to squares that serve a specific plan, not just any active square
209.description: Opening/early middlegame positions with symmetric structures. The idea: development is not just putting pieces on active squares — each piece should aim at a specific target. Develop with a PLAN, not just on autopilot.

274.label: The attack is decisive — find the killing move or combination
274.description: White to move with a strong attack, multiple checks and captures available. The position demands precision — find the move that ends the game. Dont allow counterplay by being imprecise.

294.label: Build pressure on the queenside — Qb3/Qc2, Nc3, Be2/Bb5 aiming at weak pawns
294.description: White to move with classical piece setup (Nc3+Nf3, Be2/Bg2, Qb3/Qd3). The idea: build slow positional pressure on the queenside. Target c6/c7, threaten b5, and prepare a minority attack or pawn break.

356.label: Under pressure — find the defensive move that neutralizes the threat
356.description: Black to move under positional or tactical pressure. The idea: instead of panicking, find the ONE move that solves all problems — a tactical defense, a simplifying exchange, or a counter-threat that changes the dynamics.

398.label: Use open files and diagonals — get your heavy pieces on them first
398.description: Positions where open files and diagonals are the key feature. The idea: occupy open lines FIRST. Rooks on open files, bishops on open diagonals. Whoever controls the open lines controls the game.

307.label: Target isolated, doubled, or backward pawns — they are permanent weaknesses
307.description: Positions where one side has weak pawns (isolated, doubled, backward). The idea: attack those pawns. Even if you cant win them immediately, tying down the opponents pieces to defending them gives you a free hand elsewhere.

272.label: Counter the opponents central push — challenge it or play around it
272.description: Black to move facing Whites central pressure (Qe4, Qf3, e5 pawn). The idea: dont passively accept being squeezed. Either challenge the center directly with a pawn break, or counterattack on the wing where you have more space.

261.label: Advance connected queenside passers — they create unstoppable threats
261.description: White to move with advanced queenside pawns (a/b/c files). The idea: push them! Connected passed pawns on the queenside are incredibly powerful, especially when supported by rooks. The opponent must sacrifice material to stop them.

64.label: Find your worst-placed piece and improve it — the Capablanca principle
64.description: Stable middlegame positions where no immediate tactics exist. The idea: identify your least active piece and find a better square for it. In quiet positions, the player who improves their pieces more effectively will win.

54.label: Prioritize king safety — shore up weaknesses around your king
54.description: Black to move with king under some pressure (check, pins, or threats). The idea: address king safety FIRST before any other consideration. A checkmate threat trumps everything else on the board.

349.label: Maneuver pieces to optimal squares in a closed position — patience wins
349.description: Semi-closed or closed positions where direct action is impossible. The idea: MANEUVER. Reroute pieces to better squares (Nd2-f1-e3, Bc1-b2, etc.). The player who finds the best piece arrangement wins when the position opens.

407.label: Play the forcing moves — checks, captures, threats in the right order
407.description: Positions where a forcing sequence (checks, captures, threats) decides the game. The idea: identify the correct ORDER of forcing moves. A-B-C might win, but B-A-C might lose. Sequence matters.

19.label: Choose the right response to the opponents opening move — setup determines middlegame
19.description: Very early opening positions (moves 2-5). The idea: your response to the opponents opening determines the entire character of the game. Choose a setup that leads to positions YOU understand, not what looks natural.

18.label: Find the right file or rank for your rooks — a passive rook is a dead piece
18.description: Black to move with rooks that lack open files. The critical idea: rooks need open files to function. Look for pawn trades that open lines, or reroute rooks via the back rank to files where they can penetrate. A rook sitting behind its own pawns contributes nothing. Every rook move should aim at either (a) an open file, (b) the 7th rank, or (c) defending a critical point.

240.label: A piece deep in enemy territory demands immediate action — use it or remove it
240.description: Positions where one side has a piece (knight on e7, rook on h7, queen penetrating) deep in the opponents camp. If its YOUR piece: use it as a pivot for combinations, dont let the opponent untangle. If its the opponents piece: remove it by exchange, trap it, or create a bigger threat elsewhere. Ignoring a penetrating piece is the most common error at this level.

216.label: Neutralize a powerful enemy bishop — trade it, block its diagonal, or make it bite granite
216.description: White has strong bishop(s) on central diagonals (Bd4, Be3, Bg2+Bb2). The bishops control critical squares and restrict the opponents pieces. As the side facing them: either TRADE them (especially the stronger one), block their diagonals with pawns, or reroute your pieces to squares the bishops dont control. As the side owning them: keep the position open and avoid allowing exchanges.

471.short: Use knight outposts as attack platforms
471.label: Launch operations from your knight outpost — it supports tactical breaks and piece invasions
471.description: White has a knight on a strong outpost (e5, c5, d5). The knight cant be kicked by pawns and controls key squares. The idea is NOT to just sit there — use the knight as a PLATFORM: it supports pawn breaks (f4-f5, d4-d5), covers invasion squares for rooks, and creates tactical motifs (forks, discovered attacks). The outpost is a launching pad, not a destination.

104.label: Build your entire game around the centralized knight — every piece should support or exploit it
104.description: Black has a strong knight on d5 in a Sicilian/Indian structure with pawns on d5/e6. The idea: this knight is your best piece — dont trade it unless you get something concrete in return. Place your other pieces to support it: bishops covering retreat squares, rooks on files the knight helps control, queen ready to join an attack. The knight is the strategic anchor; everything else orbits around it.

405.short: Hold the endgame — find the drawing resource
405.label: Defend the inferior endgame — look for fortress, stalemate, or perpetual check
405.description: Simplified positions with few pieces where one side is worse. The idea: dont resign mentally. Look for (1) stalemate tricks if down material, (2) fortress formations where the opponents extra material cant break through, (3) perpetual check with queen or rook, (4) trading into a drawn pawn endgame. Many theoretically lost positions are holdable with precise play.

298.label: Both sides are attacking on different wings — calculate who gets there first
298.description: Positions with kings on opposite sides or asymmetric pawn structures. Both sides have attacking chances. The critical idea: this is a RACE. Calculate concretely — dont just push pawns and hope. Who arrives first? Can you slow the opponents attack with a prophylactic move while maintaining your own? The side that combines attack with defense wins.

443.label: The opening plan depends on the pawn structure — develop pieces to serve the structure
443.description: Early opening/middlegame with full piece sets. Black must decide on a development plan. The idea: dont develop on autopilot. The PAWN STRUCTURE tells you where your pieces belong: in d4/e4 structures, Black typically wants ...Nc6-...Bd7-...Rc8 or ...Nd7-...Be7-...0-0-...b5. Wrong development wastes tempi and leads to bad middlegames.

23.label: Your knights and bishops are actively placed — use them NOW before the opponent reorganizes
23.description: Black to move with active minor pieces (knight on e4/d4, bishop on active diagonal). The idea: minor piece activity is TEMPORARY — the opponent will reroute their pieces to challenge yours. So ACT NOW: create concrete threats, force favorable trades, or win material. If you wait, your activity advantage fades.

365.label: Seize the open file with your rook — first to occupy it controls the game
365.description: Positions where an open file exists and rook placement on it is the key decision. The principle: the FIRST player to place a rook on the open file gains a lasting advantage. From there, the rook can penetrate to the 7th rank, support a passed pawn, or tie down the opponents pieces to defense. If the file is contested, double rooks on it.

376.label: Your pieces need better squares — reorganize before launching the attack
376.description: White to move in middlegame positions where pieces are not optimally placed. The idea: resist the urge to attack immediately. First REGROUP: reroute a knight from a2 to c3-e4, move a bishop to a better diagonal, centralize the queen. Attacking with poorly coordinated pieces leads to overextension. The extra time spent regrouping pays off with a stronger attack.

435.label: Down material — look for tactical tricks, perpetuals, or complications to survive
435.description: Black to move in positions where material is roughly equal or Black is slightly worse, but the position is sharp. The idea: when youre behind or under pressure, COMPLICATE. Create threats, make the opponents task harder, seek tactical complications where they can go wrong. In sharp positions, the defender who creates counter-threats has practical chances.

126.short: Contest center with rival outpost knights
126.label: Both sides have outpost knights battling for control — the one who uses theirs better wins
126.description: Black has Nd5 and White has Ne5 (or similar dual outposts). The position is a tense positional struggle: neither knight can be easily dislodged. The idea: dont just admire your knight — USE it. Support it with other pieces, launch operations on the side where your knight gives you more control. The side that coordinates better around their outpost wins the strategic battle.

3.label: White has an e5 pawn choking your position — break free with ...f6 or wing counterplay
3.description: White has advanced the e5 pawn, creating a space cramp that restricts Blacks minor pieces (especially the knight and dark-squared bishop). The critical idea: you MUST challenge this pawn or it will suffocate you. Methods: (1) ...f6 directly challenging the chain, (2) ...f5 undermining, (3) ...Nh5-f4 leaping over the pawn, (4) queenside counterplay while the center is blocked. Passive acceptance means slow death.

249.short: Press with rook on the open file
249.label: Your rook controls the only open file — use it to penetrate and create decisive threats
249.description: Positions where one side has rook(s) dominating the key open file. The opponent cannot contest it. The idea: penetrate to the 7th (or 2nd) rank where the rook attacks pawns and restricts the enemy king. If you have two rooks, double them. The open file is a highway — drive your heaviest pieces down it without stopping.

375.short: Choose your plan at the crossroads
375.label: The position is at a strategic crossroads — the plan you choose determines the entire game
375.description: Black in the early middlegame facing a critical strategic decision: castle kingside or queenside? Challenge the center with ...d5 or ...f5? Play for a kingside attack or queenside expansion? These positions require JUDGMENT, not calculation. Understand the pawn structure to determine where your pieces belong and which side to play on. The wrong plan leads to a passive, losing position.

427.label: Your knight is deep in enemy territory — it paralyzes their position, use it before they remove it
427.description: Black has a knight on c4 (or similar forward square) that has infiltrated into Whites camp. The knight attacks pawns, controls key squares, and restricts Whites pieces. The idea: this knight is TEMPORARY — eventually White will find a way to kick or trade it. So act NOW: use it to win a pawn, force favorable trades, or support a rook invasion. The clock is ticking on your advantage.

352.label: Open the long diagonal for your bishop — it becomes a monster when the center opens
352.description: White has a bishop on b2 or g2 (fianchettoed) that is currently blocked by the pawn structure. The idea: OPEN THE DIAGONAL. Trade or advance the central pawns that block it. Once the diagonal clears, the bishop becomes the strongest piece on the board — controlling squares deep in the opponents position, supporting kingside or queenside operations simultaneously.

392.label: Your queen sits in the center controlling everything — combine threats from the dominant position
392.description: Black has the queen centralized on d4, e5, or similar square where it radiates power in all directions. The idea: dont just sit — COMBINE threats. The centralized queen can pivot to attack the kingside, support piece invasions, target weak pawns, or enable tactical motifs (discovered attacks, forks). Use the queens central position to create MULTIPLE threats the opponent cant handle simultaneously.

97.label: Your king is still in the center — weigh the risk of staying vs the cost of castling
97.description: Black hasnt castled and must decide: is it safe to leave the king on e8/d8 while pursuing active play, or is castling urgent? The idea: in OPEN positions with lots of pieces, castle immediately — the king in the center is a target. In CLOSED positions with blocked pawns, the king in the center can be useful (supporting central play, saving a tempo). Read the position structure to decide.

485.label: The opponents back rank is weak — use your queen or rook to create mating threats
485.description: Positions where the opponents back rank is vulnerable (king boxed in by own pawns, no escape square, no defender on the back rank). The idea: drive your heavy pieces toward the back rank. Even if you cant checkmate immediately, the THREAT of back-rank mate forces the opponent to make concessions — giving up material, creating weaknesses, or passive defense.

254.label: A knight on the 6th rank paralyzes the opponent — it cuts their position in half
254.description: A knight on d6 or e6 (the 6th rank deep in enemy territory). This knight is devastating: it forks key squares, blocks file communication between opponents rooks, and cannot be dislodged by pawns. The idea: if its YOUR knight, protect it and use it as a platform for further operations. If its the opponents knight, removing it should be your top priority even at the cost of material.

422.label: Two well-placed knights can dominate — coordinate them to control key squares together
422.description: Positions with reduced material where two knights work together. The idea: knights complement each other beautifully — one controls the squares the other cant reach. Place them on DIFFERENT colored squares, covering each others weaknesses. In simplified positions, two coordinated knights can dominate a bishop pair by controlling specific outposts and restricting pawn advancement.

361.short: Push king deep into enemy camp
361.label: March your king to the 6th rank — in endgames it wins by controlling key squares
361.description: White king has advanced to c6/d6/e6 (or similar deep square). In the endgame, a king this deep controls promotion squares, restricts the enemy king, and supports pawn advancement. The idea: dont be afraid to walk your king forward. Every step closer to the enemy position increases your advantage exponentially.

346.short: Knight on f6 anchors the attack
346.label: A knight on f6 paralyzes the castled king — it controls g8, h7, and supports a mating attack
346.description: White has a knight firmly planted on f6. This is one of the most devastating squares in chess: it attacks h7 and g8 (trapping the king), controls e8 (cutting off escape), and cant be taken by pawns. The idea: use this knight as the ANCHOR of your attack. Every other piece should coordinate with it — queen to h5/g6, rook lift to g3/h3, bishop on the diagonal.

158.label: The bishop on b5 pins and disrupts — exploit it before the opponent breaks the pin
158.description: White has a bishop on b5 creating a pin (against the knight on c6 or king on e8). The pin restricts the opponents development and sometimes wins material directly. The idea: INCREASE the pressure on the pin. Add more pieces targeting the pinned piece (Qe2, Re1, Nc3). Dont let the opponent break the pin cheaply with ...Bd7 or ...a6.

40.label: Use opposition, key squares, and basic technique to convert the advantage
40.description: Minimal material positions (4-10 pieces). The idea: endgame fundamentals decide everything. (1) Opposition: kings facing each other with one square between — whoever does NOT have to move has the advantage. (2) Key squares: in K+P endgames, control the squares in front of the pawn. (3) Rule of the square: can the king catch the pawn? Count the distance. No tricks, just technique.

343.label: Align your pieces toward the enemy king — then break through with a pawn or piece sacrifice
343.description: White has pieces aimed at the kingside (Ng5/Nh4/Nf5, Bd3/Bc2 battery, Queen ready). The idea: first ALIGN your pieces — every piece should point at the enemy king. Then look for the breakthrough: h4-h5, g4-g5, Nxh7, Bxh7+, or a piece sacrifice to open lines. The attack succeeds only when ENOUGH pieces participate.

153.label: Both bishops fianchettoed — they exert long-range pressure, support pawn breaks from afar
153.description: White has Bb2+Bg2 (double fianchetto). The two bishops control d4/e5 and d5/c6 from a distance. The idea: dont rush to attack directly. The bishops are long-range weapons — prepare a central pawn break (c4-c5 or d4-d5) that opens lines for BOTH bishops simultaneously. The double fianchetto is a slow squeeze, not a blitz attack.

296.short: All pieces aimed at king — find the blow
296.label: Your attack is at maximum force — find the combination that breaks through NOW
296.description: All your pieces are coordinated in the attack — bishops on open diagonals, rooks on open files, queen ready, knight on an outpost. The position is ripe. The idea: CALCULATE the finishing combination. Look for piece sacrifices (Bxh7+, Nxf7, Rxg7), queen infiltration, or forcing sequences. Dont just attack generally — find the SPECIFIC winning move.

250.label: The knight on g3/g6 targets critical squares around the castled king
250.description: A knight on g3 (or g6 for Black) controls key squares: f1/h1/e2/f5 (or f8/h8/e7/f4 for Black). The idea: this knight supports a kingside attack by controlling squares near the king. Use it to (1) support a queen infiltration to h-file squares, (2) prepare a pawn break (f4-f5 or f5-f4), or (3) create fork threats. Its an attacking springboard.

300.label: Your king is on h1/h2 — watch for back-rank threats and piece infiltration
300.description: White king on h1 or h2 after a typical g3/Bg2/O-O/Kh1 setup. The danger: (1) back-rank mating threats if the g2 pawn advances, (2) piece infiltration via the g-file or f-file, (3) knight forks targeting f2/g3 squares. The idea: maintain pawn cover (keep g2 intact), ensure at least one rook defends the back rank, and be alert to tactical tricks exploiting the kings corner position.

458.label: The knight on g6 eyes f4 (attacking) or e5 (centralizing) — choose the right plan
458.description: Black has a knight on g6 in early middlegame (often KID or Pirc). The knight is well-placed but TEMPORARY — it needs a permanent home. The idea: in ATTACKING positions, maneuver it to f4 where it pressures d3/e2/g2/h3. In POSITIONAL games, reroute to e5 or d5 via e7. The knights destination depends on whether you plan to attack or consolidate.

118.label: The king hasnt castled — use the extra tempo productively or castle before its too late
118.description: The king is on e1/e2/d2 (White) or e8/d8 (Black), having not castled. The idea: an uncastled king is either a RISK or an ASSET. In closed positions with blocked centers, saving the castling tempo lets you develop faster or keep options open. In open positions, its a LIABILITY — castle immediately or face a devastating attack through the center.

66.label: Find optimal squares for your knights — each knight should target a weakness or outpost
66.description: Positions where knight placement is the key decision. Knights are short-range pieces that need SPECIFIC squares to be effective. The idea: identify the most important squares in the position (usually outposts — squares not controllable by enemy pawns) and MANEUVER your knights there. A well-placed knight is worth more than a bishop in many middlegames.

147.label: Pieces are aimed at the kingside — prepare g4-g5 or h4-h5 to open lines for the attack
147.description: White has pieces in attacking formation (Nc3, Bb3/Bc2, Nh4/Ng5, Queen available). The center is stable or closed. The idea: launch the pawn storm — g4-g5 or h4-h5 to open files and diagonals pointing at the castled king. The pawns are the battering ram; the pieces exploit the breach.

8.label: Your knight is on an aggressive square (h5/c5/c4) — use it to launch tactical operations
8.description: White has a knight on h5, c5, c4, or similar aggressive square deep in the opponents territory. The idea: the knight is perfectly placed — NOW USE IT. Look for tactical strikes: Nf6+ forks, Nd7 forks, Nxe7 captures, or simply use the knight to support a pawn advance or piece invasion. The forward knight is a loaded gun — pull the trigger.

61.label: Decide between ...d5 (solid center) or ...g6 (flexible fianchetto) — each leads to different plans
61.description: Black in the opening must choose a defensive setup. The idea: ...d5 claims central space but creates fixed pawn targets; ...g6 is flexible but concedes space. Choose based on Whites setup: against e4+d4, ...d5 challenges directly. Against slower setups, ...g6+Bg7 keeps options open. The wrong choice leads to a passive middlegame where you never find a good plan.

122.label: Multiple captures possible — only one is correct. Calculate precisely before committing.
122.description: CRITICAL positions where 4-6+ captures are available. The evaluation swings wildly depending on which one you choose. The idea: STOP and CALCULATE. Dont play the first capture you see. Check ALL captures and ALL checks in the right order. The difference between the best and second-best move can be several pawns or even the entire game.

318.label: The knight needs a better square — reroute it through the back rank (Ne7-d5, Nb6-d5, Nf1-e3)
318.description: Positions where a knight is on a sub-optimal square and needs to reach a stronger one. The idea: knight maneuvers often go BACKWARDS before going forward. Classic routes: Nf3-d2-f1-e3-d5, Nb8-d7-f8-e6, Nc3-e2-g3-f5. These maneuvers cost tempi but the DESTINATION is worth it. Patience in rerouting your knight pays off enormously.

370.label: The position is ripe for a combination — look for sacrifices, forks, and forced sequences
370.description: Sharp positions with many captures and checks available. Pieces are tangled in complex interactions. The idea: there is a FORCING SEQUENCE here that wins material or the game. Look for piece sacrifices (Bxh7+, Nxf7), queen infiltrations, discovered attacks, and zwischenzugs. Calculate ALL forcing lines before choosing.

52.label: You have positional pressure — look for the tactical moment to convert it into a concrete win
52.description: Positions where one side has built up positional pressure (better pieces, more space, weak targets). The idea: positional advantages are TEMPORARY — the opponent will reorganize if you dont act. Look for the MOMENT to convert your pressure into something concrete: winning a pawn, forcing a favorable exchange, or breaking through tactically.

332.label: The king has been forced to an unusual square — exploit its exposure or find shelter
332.description: Positions where a king sits on f7/d8/c8 (Black) or similar displaced square after losing castling rights. If its your king: find shelter, simplify, or use the king actively in the endgame. If its the opponents king: attack immediately — open lines toward it, cut off escape routes, bring more pieces into the attack before they stabilize.

379.label: The opponents pieces are uncoordinated — strike at the weak point before they regroup
379.description: Positions where one sides pieces are awkwardly placed or disconnected. Rooks not communicating, knights on bad squares, bishops blocked. The idea: identify the WEAKEST point in the opponents camp (the square or piece thats least defended) and hit it hard. Uncoordinated pieces cant help each other, so a focused strike breaks through.

482.short: Deal with the advanced pawn threat
482.label: An advanced pawn (e5/d5/e6) threatens to disrupt — decide whether to capture, block, or advance past it
482.description: Positions where one side has an advanced pawn (e5/e6/d6/c6) deep in enemy territory. This pawn cramps, disrupts piece coordination, and may promote. If its YOUR pawn: support it, use it as a wedge. If its the opponents: decide between (1) capturing it to relieve the pressure, (2) blocking it and playing around it, or (3) ignoring it and counter-attacking elsewhere.

41.label: The opponents rook has invaded — activate your own pieces to create counter-threats
41.description: Positions where the opponents rook sits on the 7th rank (or 2nd for Black) or deep in your position. The rook attacks pawns and restricts your king. The idea: DONT just defend passively. Activate your OWN rook — create counter-threats on the other side of the board. If you can generate your own rook invasion, the threats cancel out. Activity beats passivity.

367.label: Both sides have chances — balance offense and defense in this sharp position
367.description: Sharp, unbalanced positions where both sides have attacking chances. Neither side is clearly better. The idea: DONT just attack — also cover your weaknesses. And DONT just defend — keep your own threats alive. The player who balances attack and defense best wins. Prioritize forcing moves that serve BOTH purposes (attack while covering a weakness).

1.label: The center is under tension — decide: capture, advance, or maintain the tension
1.description: Opening/early middlegame with central pawn tension (e4 vs d5, d4 vs e5, etc.). The key decision: (1) CAPTURE — simplify the center but give the opponent piece activity, (2) ADVANCE — gain space but fix the pawn structure, (3) MAINTAIN TENSION — keep your options open but require more sophisticated play. The right choice depends on your development and king safety.

348.label: Rook endgame — your rook needs a better square. Activity beats material in these endings.
348.description: Rook endgame positions where rook placement is THE deciding factor. The idea: (1) Get your rook BEHIND passed pawns (yours or the opponents). (2) Keep the rook ACTIVE — a rook defending from behind is much stronger than one stuck in front of a pawn. (3) Cut off the enemy king along a rank or file. (4) Dont be afraid to sacrifice a pawn if it activates your rook.

287.label: Your advanced pawn in the center cramps the opponent — use it as a wedge for piece play
287.description: White has an advanced e5 or d5 pawn that restricts Blacks pieces. The idea: dont just rely on the pawn — USE IT. The pawn controls key squares, opening lines for your pieces. Support it with minor pieces, use the squares it creates for your knights (d6, f6), and prepare a pawn break on the flank while the center is locked.

45.label: There is a pin, skewer, or discovery in the position — find how to exploit it tactically
45.description: Positions where tactical motifs (pins, skewers, discovered attacks, x-ray attacks) are present or can be created. The idea: LOOK for these patterns. A pinned piece cant move — increase pressure on it. A discovered attack is devastating — move the blocking piece with a threat. These tactical tools convert positional advantages into material or checkmate.

188.short: Use active king to win pawn endgame
188.label: King activity is decisive — march your king forward to create and promote passed pawns
188.description: Pawn endgame or near-pawn endgame where the kings position determines everything. The idea: calculate the EXACT path for your king. Can it reach the opponents pawns? Can it support your own passed pawn? Count the moves — one tempo decides. Use triangulation and opposition to force the opponent into zugzwang.

368.label: The pawn structure is being determined NOW — choose the formation that suits your pieces
368.description: Opening/early middlegame positions where pawn moves will fix the structure for the rest of the game. The idea: look at your PIECES first, then choose the pawn structure that suits them. Bishops want open diagonals (advance pawns to clear them). Knights want outposts (create pawn holes for them). Rooks want open files (exchange pawns to create them).

197.label: The opponents pieces are still at home — strike NOW before they organize their defense
197.description: Positions where one side has a big lead in development. The opponent has pieces on their starting squares or poorly placed. The idea: TIME is your weapon. Open the position with pawn breaks or sacrifices. Every move you spend NOT attacking wastes your development advantage. The opponents undeveloped pieces cant help defend — make them pay.

283.label: Your knight on d4 controls the board — it restricts the opponent and supports your operations
283.description: White has a strong knight on d4. This knight controls b5, c6, e6, f5 — key squares in the opponents camp. The idea: KEEP the knight there. Support it with pawns (c3, e3) and pieces. Use it as a base for operations: rook lifts (Ra3-h3), pawn storms (f4-f5), or piece maneuvers. The d4 knight is your strategic anchor.

310.label: The opponent has a backward pawn — place a piece in front of it and attack it down the file
310.description: Positions where one side has a backward pawn (a pawn that cant be supported by neighboring pawns and sits on a semi-open file). The idea: (1) Place a knight or bishop on the square in front of the backward pawn — it becomes an impregnable outpost. (2) Double rooks on the file targeting the pawn. (3) Force the opponent to defend it permanently, tying down their pieces.

39.label: Knight fork threats are in the air — use them to win material or create decisive threats
39.description: Positions where knight forks are possible or can be created. The knight attacks in an L-shape, meaning it can threaten two pieces at once. The idea: look for squares where your knight attacks the king + queen, king + rook, or queen + rook simultaneously. Sometimes a preparatory move is needed to set up the fork.

256.label: Enemy pieces are invading — find the defensive resource that neutralizes the threats
256.description: Black to move facing Whites piece activity in the opening. White has knights and bishops aggressively placed, often with pins (Bb5) or central pressure (Nd5, Ne5). The idea: dont panic. Look for (1) breaking the pin with ...Bd7 or ...a6, (2) counter-pinning, (3) challenging the invading piece directly with ...Nxe5, or (4) counter-attacking in the center.

191.label: Multiple captures are available — evaluate each one to find the best recapture or intermediate move
191.description: Positions with 3+ captures available. The order of captures matters enormously. The idea: dont automatically recapture. Consider: (1) Is there an intermediate move (zwischenzug) thats stronger? (2) Which capture improves your pawn structure? (3) Which capture opens lines for your pieces? (4) Can you capture with CHECK? The wrong capture order can lose the game.

317.label: Your king is on the queenside — use the kingside for a counter-attack
317.description: Black with king on c8/d8 (queenside). White is attacking. The idea: when your king is being attacked, the best defense is often a counter-attack on the OPPOSITE side. Open files toward the White king (if castled kingside), create threats that force White to divert resources from the attack.

311.label: A complex exchange sequence is available — calculate it to the end before committing
311.description: Positions where a sequence of exchanges (captures, recaptures, intermediate moves) determines the outcome. The idea: calculate the ENTIRE sequence before playing the first move. Count material at the end. Check for intermediate checks, zwischenzugs, and defensive resources the opponent has in the sequence.

411.label: The opponent is cramped — increase the pressure before they unravel
411.description: Positions where one side has significantly less space. Pieces are tripping over each other, lacking good squares. The idea: DONT let them uncramp. Maintain the pressure by (1) controlling the squares they need for maneuvers, (2) threatening pawn breaks that further restrict, (3) provoking weaknesses they cant avoid. A cramped position eventually collapses.

279.label: Many pieces in contact — resolve the tension at the right moment, not too early
279.description: Dense middlegame with multiple pieces in tension (attacking/defending each other). The idea: tension is POWER — the side that resolves it prematurely usually gets the worse position. Maintain it while improving your position. When you DO resolve it, make sure its on YOUR terms — capture in a way that favors your pawn structure and piece activity.

378.label: Knight vs bishop — exploit the knights ability to reach squares the bishop cant
378.description: Endgame or simplified middlegame with knight vs bishop. The idea: if you have the knight, put pawns on BOTH sides of the board and create positions where the bishop is restricted by its own pawns or the pawn structure. If you have the bishop, keep the position OPEN and create passed pawns on one wing.

388.label: Both sides are grabbing material — make sure you come out ahead in the exchange
388.description: Positions where both sides are capturing and counter-capturing. Material is flying off the board. The idea: count PRECISELY. After all the dust settles, who has more? Look for in-between moves that gain a tempo during the exchange. Sometimes sacrificing material during the sequence leads to a decisive advantage.

474.label: Limit the opponents piece activity — tie down their pieces to passive defense
474.description: Positions where one sides pieces are restricted. The idea: keep them that way. (1) Control the squares they need to activate. (2) Create threats on multiple fronts so they cant reorganize. (3) Slowly improve YOUR pieces while theirs are stuck. Eventually the positional bind becomes material or tactical.

268.label: Each developing move should create a concrete threat — dont develop to passive squares
268.description: Opening/early middlegame where development quality matters more than quantity. The idea: each piece move should DO something — threaten a pawn, control a key square, support a pawn break, or create a tactical motif. Developing to passive squares (like Bd3 blocking your own d-pawn) wastes the tempo advantage.

325.label: You lead in development — open the position NOW before the opponent catches up
325.description: Positions where one side has more pieces developed. The key insight: a development lead is a WASTING asset — it disappears as the opponent catches up. So you must ACT immediately: sacrifice a pawn to open lines, play a central break, or start an attack. The clock is ticking on your advantage.

37.label: A rook on the 7th rank attacks pawns, restricts the king, and dominates — use it to the fullest
37.description: White has a rook on the 7th rank (or Black on the 2nd). This is one of the most powerful piece placements in chess. The idea: the rook attacks all the opponents pawns from behind, restricts the king to the back rank, and supports your own passed pawn advancement. If possible, DOUBLE rooks on the 7th for a decisive advantage.

453.label: You have a passed pawn — advance it with support from your pieces
453.description: Positions with an advanced passed pawn that threatens promotion. The idea: the passed pawn is your most dangerous weapon. Support it with (1) the king (in endgames), (2) rooks from behind, (3) minor pieces escorting it. The opponent must sacrifice material to stop it — use that sacrifice to win elsewhere.

11.label: Open lines on the kingside to expose the castled king — sacrifice a pawn if necessary
11.description: White to move with pieces aimed at the kingside. The kings pawn shelter can be broken. The idea: sacrifice a pawn (Bxh7+, g4-g5, h4-h5) to rip open the pawn cover around the enemy king. Once lines are open, your pieces flood in. The sacrifice is usually sound if you have 3+ pieces aimed at the kingside.

82.label: Many pieces, many plans — find the move that improves your position on multiple fronts
82.description: Complex middlegame with full piece sets and multiple plans available. The idea: find the move that serves MULTIPLE purposes — improves a piece AND creates a threat AND prepares a pawn break. Such moves are objectively strongest because they give the opponent no easy response. Avoid one-dimensional moves.

355.label: In the Pirc/Modern — dont rush to challenge the center, first complete the fianchetto setup
355.description: Black to move in Pirc/Modern Defense (g6+Bg7+d6+e6). Whites center looks imposing (e4+d4). The idea: dont panic about the center. Complete your setup (...Nf6, ...0-0, ...Nbd7 or ...Nc6), then challenge the center at the right moment with ...e5, ...c5, or ...d5. Premature pawn breaks fail; patient preparation works.

468.label: In the pawn endgame every move matters — calculate the promotion race precisely
468.description: Pure or near-pure pawn endings. The idea: this is 100%% CALCULATION. (1) Can you create a passed pawn? (2) Can the opponents king stop it? (3) Is there opposition? (4) Can you force zugzwang? Count moves, dont guess. One wrong move draws a won position or loses a drawn one.

266.label: The knight on g5 targets f7/h7 — look for sacrifices and tactical shots on the kingside
266.description: White has a knight on g5 attacking f7 (the weakest square in Blacks position). The idea: the Ng5 creates immediate tactical threats — Nxf7 (forking queen and rook), Qxh7# ideas, Bxf7+ discoveries. Even if the sacrifice isnt immediately sound, the THREAT forces Black into passive defense.

486.label: Your pieces are tripping over each other — find the right move order to unravel the mess
486.description: Positions where pieces are awkwardly placed (knights on the rim, bishops blocked, rooks disconnected). The idea: identify the MOST restricted piece and find a path to improve it. Often you need to move OTHER pieces out of the way first. The right untangling sequence matters — one wrong move order and you stay stuck.

395.label: Your bishop controls key squares — use it to restrict the opponents king and support your pawns
395.description: Simplified positions with bishop vs knight or bishop vs pawns. The idea: the bishop is a LONG-RANGE piece. Use it to control squares on the opposite side of the board from the king, create distant threats, and support passed pawns from afar. Put your pawns on the OPPOSITE color of your bishop to maximize coverage.

461.label: The opponents queen is aggressively placed — find defensive resources before it becomes fatal
461.description: Black to move facing Whites queen creating threats (Qh7, Qg6, Qe6). The idea: against an aggressive queen, look for (1) queen exchanges that defuse the attack, (2) defensive interposition moves, (3) counter-attacks forcing the queen to retreat. A lone queen without piece support can often be repelled.

62.label: The center was disrupted — re-establish control with pieces and pawns
62.description: Positions after central exchanges where the center is fluid. The idea: whoever controls the center after the dust settles gets the better middlegame. Re-occupy central squares with pieces (Nd4, Be4), support with pawns (c4, e4), and dont let the opponent plant a strong piece in the center unchallenged.

260.short: React to pawn exchange in center
260.label: A central pawn was captured — decide the best recapture that improves your position
260.description: Black to move after a central exchange (exd5, dxe5, etc). The recapture choice shapes the entire game: (1) piece recapture opens lines, (2) pawn recapture maintains structure. The idea: choose based on what your PIECES need — if they need open lines, recapture with a piece. If they need outposts, recapture with a pawn.

456.label: Unequal material — use the unique strengths of what you have
456.description: Positions with material imbalances (rook vs knight+pawn, queen vs two rooks, bishop vs pawns). The idea: each piece has unique strengths. Rooks love open files; bishops love open diagonals; knights love closed positions with outposts; queens love open positions. STEER the game toward positions that favor YOUR material.

263.label: Your central pawns (d4+d5+e4) control the board — advance them or use them to restrict
263.description: White with a powerful pawn center (d4+d5, d4+e4, or d5+e5). The idea: the pawn center is a weapon — use it to (1) cramp the opponent, (2) support outpost squares for your pieces, (3) create a passed pawn by advancing at the right moment. But dont advance prematurely — the pawns need piece support.

120.label: Your queen is your most active piece — use it to create threats that force the opponent to react
120.description: Black to move with an active queen that can create tactical threats. The idea: the queen is the most powerful attacking piece. Use it to (1) attack undefended pawns, (2) create mating threats against the king, (3) fork pieces, (4) support piece invasions. Keep it active and threatening — a passive queen is useless.

90.label: Your bishop on c4 targets f7 — combine with Nf3/Qb3 to create concrete pressure
90.description: White has Bc4 aimed at f7 (the weakest point in Blacks starting position). The idea: build a BATTERY along the diagonal. Qb3 adds pressure on f7 and b7. Ng5 adds more. The f7 square is defended only by the king — enough pressure forces concessions or wins material.

244.label: Isolated queen pawn (IQP) — use its dynamic potential before it becomes a weakness
244.description: Positions with an isolated d-pawn. The idea: the IQP is a DOUBLE-EDGED sword. FOR the IQP: the pawn controls c5/e5 squares and gives piece activity; play dynamically before the endgame. AGAINST the IQP: blockade the pawn on d5 with a knight, exchange pieces to reach an endgame where the isolated pawn becomes a target.

162.label: The opponents king is exposed — find the sequence that creates an unstoppable mating net
162.description: Positions where the opponents king has weaknesses in its pawn cover or limited escape squares. The idea: direct your pieces toward the king and look for mating patterns — back rank mates, smothered mates, queen+knight mates on h7/g7, and rook lifts to the h-file. Sometimes a quiet move (cutting off the escape) is stronger than a check.

206.label: The opponent castled queenside — attack on the a/b/c files with pawn storm and piece activity
206.description: Black has king on c8/c7 (queenside castled). The idea: attack on the QUEENSIDE with pawns (a5-a4, b5-b4) to open files, and pieces (rook on the a or b file, queen supporting). Pawn storms are effective because the defenders pawns are the shield — break the shield and the king is exposed.

178.label: Your bishop dominates the dark squares — use it to restrict the opponents movement
178.description: Black has a powerful bishop on a dark-square diagonal (e5, d4, g7). The idea: a dominant bishop controls squares the opponents knight and king need. Keep it on its strong diagonal, dont trade it unless you get something concrete. The opponents light-squared weaknesses will grow as long as your bishop patrols the dark squares.

125.label: Pure king and pawn endgame — use opposition and key square theory to promote
125.description: K+P endgame positions. The idea: (1) The OPPOSITION determines who controls the key squares in front of the pawn. (2) If your king reaches the 6th rank in front of your pawn, you win. (3) Count the distance — can the opponents king reach your pawn? (4) Look for zugzwang positions. Every tempo matters.

144.short: Defend the R vs R+P endgame
144.label: Rook endgame with extra pawn — cut off the king or activate your rook to hold
144.description: Rook endgame where one side has an extra pawn. The idea: as the DEFENDER, (1) keep your rook ACTIVE (checking from behind), (2) cut off the opponents king from the pawn, (3) use the Philidor defense if the pawn hasnt reached the 6th rank. As the attacker: get your king in front of the pawn and push with rook support from behind.

487.label: The opponents king is exposed — coordinate your pieces to create decisive threats
487.description: Positions where the opponents king has lost its pawn shelter or is stuck in the center. The idea: every piece should aim at the king. Rooks on open files toward the king, bishops on diagonals pointing at it, knights hopping to attacking squares. Coordinate — a scattered attack fails, but a coordinated one breaks through.

478.label: Under pressure — find the ONLY move that holds the position together
478.description: Black to move in positions where the defense is razor-thin. Many of Whites pieces are attacking, and most Black moves lose. The idea: in critical defensive positions, there is often ONE move that holds — a quiet defensive move, an exchange sacrifice, or a counter-threat. Dont panic; systematically check each candidate move until you find the one that works.

89.label: The opening has become sharp — calculate concretely rather than playing on general principles
89.description: Complex opening positions where general principles (develop, castle, control center) arent enough. The position demands CONCRETE calculation. The idea: when the position is tactical (pieces en prise, forks available, pins present), stop thinking about principles and START calculating. Find the specific move that works.

277.label: You are in a critical opening line — the next few moves determine the entire game
277.description: Opening positions at a theoretical crossroads (Sicilian, Italian, Queens Gambit critical lines). The idea: these positions have been analyzed deeply — the correct moves are SPECIFIC, not general. If you know the theory, follow it. If you dont, apply the principles: develop quickly, control the center, keep the king safe, and dont grab poisoned pawns.

53.label: In the Dragon/Pirc — your fianchettoed bishop is your main weapon, keep it alive
53.description: Black in Sicilian Dragon or Pirc Defense with g6+Bg7+d6 setup. The Bg7 bishop controls the long diagonal and is Blacks best piece. The idea: NEVER trade this bishop unless you get a crushing advantage. White will try to exchange it (Bh6) — avoid the trade or ensure compensation. Build counterplay on the queenside (b5-b4) while defending the kingside.

184.label: Queens Gambit middlegame — play with the isolated d-pawn dynamic or the blocked center
184.description: Classical QGD middlegame with Bd3+Be3+Nf3 (or similar). The idea depends on the pawn structure: (1) If White has an IQP (d4 isolated): play dynamically with piece activity before the endgame. (2) If the center is blocked (d4 vs d5): maneuver and prepare a pawn break. (3) If the center is open: use piece activity and central control.

334.short: Convert the attack into a win
334.label: Your attack is strong but not yet decisive — find the precise continuation that forces the win
334.description: White has a strong attack with active pieces, but the winning move requires precision. The idea: dont play the obvious aggressive move — look for the PRECISE one. Sometimes its a quiet move (cutting off the king), sometimes a sacrifice (opening the last barrier), sometimes a zwischenzug (an in-between move that improves your attack).

36.label: You have both bishops — open the position so they can dominate together
36.description: White has the bishop pair (two bishops vs bishop+knight or two knights). The idea: bishops are LONG-RANGE pieces that get stronger in OPEN positions. So (1) trade pawns to open lines, (2) avoid blocking your own bishops diagonals with pawns, (3) place the bishops on parallel diagonals (one dark, one light) for maximum coverage. The bishop pair is worth ~half a pawn extra.

387.label: Both sides have active knights — maneuver yours to the superior square
387.description: Positions where both sides have active knights in reduced material. The key battle is whose knight ends up on the better square. Maneuver your knight to an outpost the opponent cant challenge with pawns. In endgames with knights, pawn structure matters enormously — knights need outposts to function.

214.label: Down to very few pieces — find the exact defensive technique to draw or survive
214.description: Minimal material positions where every move matters. The defender must find exact moves — opposition in K+P endgames, back-rank defense with rooks, or fortress construction. One tempo mistake and the game is lost. Calculate precisely, dont guess.

81.label: Your queenside pawns outnumber the opponents — advance them to create a passed pawn
81.description: White has more pawns on the queenside (a+b+c files) and can use them to create a passed pawn. The idea: advance the majority (b4-b5, a4-a5, c5-c6) to create a passer while your pieces keep the opponent busy on the kingside. A distant passed pawn draws defensive resources away.

413.label: Material is unbalanced after a sacrifice — evaluate whether the compensation is sufficient
413.description: Positions where a piece sacrifice has occurred or is possible. One side has extra material but the other has piece activity, attacking chances, or positional compensation. The idea: OBJECTIVELY evaluate — is the compensation real or illusory? If you sacrificed: act fast before the opponent consolidates. If you accepted: simplify to reach a position where the extra material speaks.

190.label: The opponent is playing aggressively in the opening — find the refutation or safe response
190.description: Early middlegame where one side has played aggressively (pawn storms, piece sallies, gambit play). The idea: aggressive play often has a concrete refutation — a counter-stroke in the center, a tactical trick, or simply calm development that leaves the attacker overextended. Dont panic; objectively evaluate whether the aggression is sound.

2.label: The opponents pawn structure has been damaged — target the weaknesses permanently
2.description: Positions where one sides pawn structure is compromised (doubled pawns, isolated pawns, backward pawns, pawn holes). The idea: structural weaknesses are PERMANENT — they dont heal. Plant pieces on the weak squares, target weak pawns with rooks, and steer toward an endgame where the structural damage is decisive.

204.label: Your queen is the most active piece — place it where it serves both attack and defense
204.description: Positions where queen placement is the key decision. The idea: the queen should (1) control key central squares, (2) threaten enemy weaknesses, (3) support your own operations, AND (4) remain safe from harassment by enemy minor pieces. A queen that serves multiple purposes is far stronger than one focused on a single threat.

496.label: All pieces working together — maintain the pressure and look for the break
496.description: Positions where all your pieces are well-coordinated and applying pressure. The idea: dont rush to break through. MAINTAIN the pressure — the opponent will eventually crack under sustained accurate play. Look for small improvements (moving a piece from a good square to a great square) while keeping all threats alive.

439.label: Knight or bishop endgame — the right minor piece wins based on the pawn structure
439.description: Endgames with knight(s) and/or bishop(s) plus pawns. The idea: (1) Bishops favor OPEN positions with pawns on both wings. (2) Knights favor CLOSED positions with fixed pawn structures. (3) In B vs N: the side with the bishop should open the position; the side with the knight should close it. (4) Same-colored bishops can lead to fortresses.

140.label: Your position is worse but not lost — find resources to fight back or hold
140.description: Positions where one side is worse but has practical chances. The idea: (1) Dont play passively hoping the opponent blunders. (2) Create counter-threats, even small ones. (3) Complicate if youre losing — in sharp positions the better player can overcome a material deficit. (4) Look for drawing mechanisms (perpetual check, fortress, stalemate).

324.label: You have the initiative — keep making threats so the opponent never gets to play their plan
324.description: Positions where one side has the initiative (dictating play, forcing responses). The idea: the initiative is like a hot potato — if you stop making threats, the opponent seizes it. Every move should either (1) create a new threat, (2) improve a piece while maintaining existing threats, or (3) force a favorable transition. Dont let the pressure drop.

286.label: Deep Sicilian middlegame — both sides have chances, concrete play decides
286.description: Rich Sicilian middlegame positions with opposite-side castling, central tension, and mutual attacking chances. The idea: this is not about general principles — its about CONCRETE PLAY. Calculate specific variations. Typical plans: White attacks on the kingside (g4-g5, Bh6, Nd5); Black counterattacks on the queenside (b5-b4, Rc8, Qa5).

301.label: Bishop on b5 creates lasting pressure — use it to disrupt the opponents development
301.description: White has Bb5 applying pressure on c6/d7 squares. The bishop pins or restrains Black pieces. The idea: maintain the bishop on b5 as long as its useful (dont capture on c6 prematurely). The longer it stays, the more it disrupts Blacks coordination. Only trade when it opens a file or creates a concrete structural advantage.

505.label: A piece sacrifice has been offered in the opening — evaluate whether to accept or decline
505.description: Sharp opening positions where a sacrifice (gambit pawn, piece sacrifice) is on the table. The idea: CALCULATE whether accepting is safe. Key questions: (1) Can the opponent prove compensation with concrete threats? (2) Can you return material later to neutralize the attack? (3) Is declining better — maintaining solid development? Dont accept on autopilot.

488.label: An enemy piece has no escape squares — trap it or exploit its immobility
488.description: Positions where a piece (usually a knight or bishop) has limited escape squares and can potentially be trapped. The idea: (1) Identify pieces that are running out of squares. (2) Cut off their retreat routes with pawns or pieces. (3) Even if you cant capture the trapped piece, its immobility means the opponent is effectively playing with one less piece.

95.short: Use the queen for tactical strikes
95.label: Your queen can create immediate tactical threats — look for forks, pins, and mating ideas
95.description: Positions where the queen has access to multiple strong squares. The idea: the queen COMBINED with a minor piece or rook is devastating. Look for (1) queen + knight forks, (2) queen + bishop battery on a diagonal, (3) queen infiltration via weak squares around the king. The queens versatility means there are always multiple threats to consider.

267.label: Your rook controls the open file pointing at the enemy king — break through on that file
267.description: Rooks on open files aimed at the enemy kings position. The idea: the rook on the open file is your battering ram. Support it with a second rook (doubled rooks), add queen pressure, and look for the BREAK — a sacrifice or pawn advance that opens the position and lets the rook penetrate to the 7th/8th rank.

85.short: Play the rook and minor piece endgame
85.label: R+B or R+N endgame — coordinate the pieces to attack or defend weak pawns
85.description: Endgames with rook + minor piece vs rook + minor piece (plus pawns). The idea: the ROOK should be active (attacking weak pawns, cutting off the king). The minor piece should support — a bishop covers one color complex, a knight covers the holes. Coordinate them: rook attacks, minor piece defends (or vice versa). Dont let the opponent create a passed pawn unopposed.

51.label: The opponents knight on e5 is powerful — challenge it with ...Nd7, ...f6, or a pawn break
51.description: Black facing White Ne5. This knight controls d7, f7, c6, g6 — critical squares. The idea: you MUST challenge it or it will dominate forever. Methods: (1) ...Nd7 directly challenging, (2) ...f6 kicking it with a pawn, (3) ...Nxe5 followed by ...d5 equalizing, (4) ignoring it and counter-attacking elsewhere (risky). Leaving it unchallenged means slow positional death.

86.label: Your pieces work together beautifully — look for the combination that proves the coordination
86.description: Positions where one side has superior piece coordination (pieces aiming at the same target, supporting each other). The idea: coordination is proved by COMBINATIONS. A discovered attack, a deflection, a pin exploiting the harmony of your pieces. The opponent cannot defend everything simultaneously when all your pieces threaten the same point.

270.label: Target f7 (or f2) — its only defended by the king and is the weakest point in the starting position
270.description: Positions where f7 (for Black) or f2 (for White) is under pressure. The idea: f7/f2 is the Achilles heel — defended only by the king in the opening. Build a BATTERY targeting it (Bc4+Qb3, Ng5+Qh5, or Rxf7 sacrifice). Even if you dont win material, threatening f7 forces defensive concessions.

166.label: A piece is pinned — increase pressure on it until it collapses or the opponent makes concessions
166.description: Positions with a pin (a piece unable to move because it would expose a more valuable piece). The idea: PILE UP on the pinned piece. Add more attackers. The defender must add more defenders, tying down their pieces. Eventually the defense breaks — either the pin wins material or the tied-down pieces allow you to break through elsewhere.

408.label: The opponents back rank is weak — threaten mate or force defensive concessions
408.description: Positions where the opponents back rank lacks defenders (king boxed in by pawns, no luft). The idea: even if you cant mate immediately, the THREAT of back-rank mate forces the opponent to make a weakening move (h6/g6) or keep a piece defending passively. Use this leverage to win material or infiltrate.

506.label: The opponents attack lacks support — find the counter that proves its unsound
506.description: Positions where one side has launched an attack without enough preparation. The idea: premature attacks fail when met with CENTRAL COUNTER-PLAY. If the attacker has pushed pawns forward, the center is weak — break it open. If pieces are advanced alone, they can be harried backwards. The refutation is almost always in the center.

351.label: Your central pawns supported by pieces — advance them at the right moment to gain decisive space
351.description: White has a central pawn duo (e4+d5, d4+e5, or c4+d5) supported by pieces. The idea: the pawns WANT to advance, but timing is everything. First: complete development and ensure king safety. Then: look for the moment when the pawn advance gains space, opens lines for your pieces, and restricts the opponents play.

477.short: Attack with the d5 pawn wedge
477.label: Your d5 pawn splits the opponents position — use it as a base for piece operations
477.description: White has a d5 pawn deep in Blacks territory. This pawn (1) controls c6 and e6, (2) cuts Blacks position in half, (3) restricts the bishop and knight. The idea: support the pawn with pieces and use the squares it creates (c6, e6) as outposts for knights or rooks. The d5 wedge is a long-term strategic weapon.

142.label: Your rook on the 7th rank cuts off the king and devours pawns — exploit this domination
142.description: A rook on the 7th rank (2nd for Black) attacks all undefended pawns and restricts the opposing king to the back rank. If possible, DOUBLE rooks on the 7th — this is often immediately winning. The opponents pieces must passively defend, giving you a free hand elsewhere.

366.label: The opponent attacks on one wing — counter-strike on the other or in the center
366.description: Positions where one side attacks a flank while the other side must find counterplay. The classic principle: a flank attack is best met by a central counter-strike (d5!, e5!). If the center is locked, counter-attack on the opposite wing. The key is TIMING — strike before the opponents attack becomes overwhelming.

397.label: Every piece should aim at a single target — concentrated force breaks through
397.description: Positions where coordinated piece play is the theme. The idea: dont spread your pieces across the board. CONCENTRATE them against one weakness. When three or four pieces all attack the same point, the defense eventually collapses. Regroup any piece thats not contributing to the main plan.

149.label: Your bishop outperforms the opponents knight in this structure — keep the position open
149.description: Positions where a bishop is clearly superior to a knight (open diagonals, pawns on both wings). The idea: KEEP the position open. Trade pawns, avoid creating closed structures where the knight would shine. The bishops long-range ability to influence both wings simultaneously is your advantage.

199.label: Endgame — but there are still threats to create. Activate pieces and push passed pawns.
199.description: Simplified positions that still have dynamic potential. The idea: endgames arent just technique — they require ACTIVE play. Create passed pawns, activate your king aggressively, and look for tactical tricks. A passive approach in the endgame lets the opponent improve until they break through.

415.label: One of your pieces is pinned — break the pin or use it constructively
415.description: Positions where a pin restricts a piece. The idea: (1) Break the pin by interposing, moving the back piece, or capturing the pinning piece. (2) If you cant break it, minimize the damage by not placing more pieces in the pin line. (3) Sometimes you can IGNORE the pin temporarily if you have a bigger threat.

127.label: A mating pattern exists — recognize it and force the checkmate
127.description: Positions where a forced checkmate is possible with the right sequence. Common patterns: back rank mate, smothered mate (Nf7-Nh6-Ng8), queen + knight coordination on h7/g7, and rook lift mates (Rh3-Rh8#). The idea: recognize the PATTERN first, then calculate the exact move order.

211.label: Your passed pawn is far from the opponents king — advance it to draw defenders away
211.description: An outside passed pawn (on the a or h file, far from the action). The idea: advance it! The opponent must divert their king or pieces to stop it, leaving your king free to win material on the other side. An outside passed pawn is worth more than its actual value because of the DISTRACTION it creates.

400.label: You have more pieces developed — open the position to use your development lead
400.description: Opening/early middlegame where one side leads significantly in development. The idea: development is TEMPORARY — use it NOW. Open the position with pawn breaks or sacrifices. Every undeveloped piece on the opponents back rank is one less defender. The goal: create concrete threats before the opponent catches up.

20.label: Your rook is more active than the opponents — use it to create threats or win material
20.description: Positions where rook activity is the key differentiator. An active rook (controlling an open file, on the 7th rank, cutting off the king) is worth significantly more than a passive one. The idea: maintain your rooks activity at all costs — even sacrificing a pawn to keep it active can be worthwhile.

25.label: Queen endgame — use checks and threats to promote your pawns or force the opponents king into trouble
25.description: Endgames with queens and pawns. The idea: queen endgames are SHARP — the queen can create perpetual check, attack pawns from distance, and support passed pawn advancement simultaneously. Key principle: the side with the more advanced passed pawn usually wins because the queen can support promotion from afar while creating mating threats.

15.label: Sicilian positions with reduced material — piece activity and pawn structure determine the evaluation
15.description: Sicilian middlegame/endgame positions where material is roughly equal but piece activity differs. The idea: in Sicilians, piece ACTIVITY trumps structure. An active knight on d5 or rook on the c-file can be worth more than good pawn structure. Look for concrete tactical chances rather than playing positionally.

479.label: The endgame is complex with multiple factors — calculate precisely and activate your pieces
479.description: Complicated endgames with multiple pawns and pieces where the evaluation isnt clear. The idea: (1) Calculate concrete variations — dont rely on general principles. (2) Activate your pieces FIRST, then worry about pawns. (3) Create a passed pawn if possible. (4) Centralize your king. Every endgame comes down to: king activity, pawn advancement, and piece coordination.

273.label: Your pieces are more active — convert the activity into something concrete before it fades
273.description: Positions where one side has clearly more active pieces. The idea: piece activity is a temporary advantage — the opponent will reorganize. So convert it NOW: win a pawn, force a favorable exchange, break through tactically, or transition to a winning endgame. Dont just admire your active pieces — USE them.

403.label: The position is ripe for a decisive tactic — find the move that wins material or forces mate
403.description: Positions where a tactical blow exists that wins the game. The idea: all the buildup has led to THIS moment. Find the specific move — a sacrifice, a fork, a discovered attack, or a quiet move that creates an unstoppable threat. This is where preparation meets calculation. Take your time and find the killer.

340.label: Sharp Sicilian with mutual chances — concrete calculation is required, not general play
